summary.text: A 44-year-old female patient had granulomatosis with polyangiitis diagnosed five months earlier, with upper and lower respiratory tract involvement, positive c-ANCA, chronic unspecific inflammation on nasal mucosa biopsy and no renal involvement. Imaging showed bilateral lung nodules, sinus and ear changes, and CT of the skull and sinuses showed bilateral mastoiditis and pansinusitis. Cyclophosphamide and methylprednisolone gave an unsatisfactory response.

Over time her symptoms did not improve, with worsening exophthalmia, drowsiness and apathy. She was admitted and started on rituximab. On the first hospital day she had drowsiness and a tonic-clonic seizure, then bradycardia of 32 bpm and hypotension. In the cardiovascular intensive care unit a bedside electrocardiogram showed complete atrioventricular heart block with multiple episodes of sustained ventricular tachycardia on monitoring.

Echocardiography showed no important morphological abnormality apart from mild mitral regurgitation with an ejection fraction of 62%, and troponin and pro-BNP were normal while C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate were elevated. Cardiac MRI and myocardial biopsy were not performed. A provisory transvenous pacemaker gave immediate improvement, she recovered consciousness, and the authors judged granulomatosis with polyangiitis with cardiac involvement the most likely cause.

She started rituximab weekly for four weeks, had no further ventricular tachycardia after six days, was still pacemaker dependent and received a permanent pacemaker. She was discharged after antibiotics for pneumonia, rituximab was resumed, and CD19 B lymphocytes were near zero. After 6 months markers normalized and the pacemaker was turned off; she remains in Rheumatology and Cardiology follow-up awaiting removal.

article_limitations: Figure pixels were inspected in a separate visual submission; values printed inside images (the Figure 5 timeline dates, monitor text) are pixel content and are not facts or conflict sides.

The Figure 5 timeline places the first symptoms, diagnosis, worsening, admission and later events in printed months; the text gives only "five months ago" for the diagnosis, and the printed dates are not used as time values.

The monitor printout in Figure 3B carries a printed recording date that falls before the admission month printed in the Figure 5 timeline; the discrepancy is not reconciled and the printed date is not used as a fact.
The case section has typographical gaps (a sentence without a printed subject, "imagem exams", "troponi", "heat block"); wording is preserved in quotes and not corrected.
Table 1 day columns have no named anchor; missing cells (CPK, CKMB and troponin I on Days 3 and 5, phosphorus on Day 19) are not values.
Discussion sentences about granulomatosis with polyangiitis in general (frequencies, treatments, cardiac manifestations, literature cases) are background and not patient facts.

Parent review: the Figure 3B printout and Figure 4 radiographs carry burned-in identifiers and a recording date (flagged in the privacy sidecar, values not copied); the Figure 5 month labels are authored timeline text and are not used as times.
